column5: CMA207: in the UK, from 6 April 2025 unfair commercial practices are governed by Chapter 1 of Part 4 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, which replaced the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008 with much the same scope plus new rules on fake reviews and drip pricing. Two kinds: 32 practices banned in all circumstances (Schedule 20) plus omitting required information from an invitation to purchase; and misleading actions, misleading omissions, aggressive practices and breaches of professional diligence, which are unfair if likely to change the average consumer's decision. Module 6 currently teaches only the Irish rules.

CMA207 core concepts: a trader is anyone acting for business purposes, including agents and representatives acting for the business; a consumer is an individual acting wholly or mainly outside their business; a 'transactional decision' includes decisions before any purchase, such as whether to agree to a sales presentation, visit a shop or click through, and decisions after it, such as whether to cancel or pay. So a salesperson's call itself is a commercial practice.

CMA207 scope: business-to-business dealings that cannot affect consumers fall outside the unfair commercial practices rules, but the trader should then consider the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008; a supplier to retailers must still make truthful claims if they reach consumers. Corrects the course's implication that B2B selling has no misleading-marketing law.

CMA207 vulnerable and targeted consumers: a practice is judged from the average member of a group the trader could reasonably foresee is vulnerable because of age, physical or mental health, credulity or circumstances (for example bereavement, divorce or job loss); the test is objective, so it is enough that the trader could have foreseen it; examples include burglar alarm sales to elderly people. The average consumer is reasonably well informed, observant and circumspect, and cannot be expected to research what the trader hides.

CMA207 banned practices most relevant to a salesperson (Schedule 20 DMCC Act): 7 falsely saying a product or terms are available only for a limited time to force an immediate decision (a countdown that restarts); 11 presenting legal rights, such as the 14-day cancellation right, as a special feature of your offer; 14 exaggerating risks to the consumer's safety if they do not buy; 17 false closing-down or moving claims; 20 false information about market conditions or availability; 23 calling something 'free' when the consumer must pay more than delivery or response costs; 25 posing as a consumer or private seller; 26 creating the impression the consumer cannot leave until they sign; 27 ignoring a request to leave or not return to the consumer's home; 28 persistent and unwanted solicitations by phone, email or other means (a TPS-registered consumer is treated as not wanting unsolicited calls); 32 telling the consumer your job or livelihood is at risk if they do not buy.

CMA207 enforcement: breaches of banned practices can lead to compliance directions and monetary penalties up to the higher of 300,000 pounds or 10% of worldwide turnover, and most banned practices (all except paragraphs 12, 13 and 30) are also criminal offences that can lead to fines or imprisonment.

CMA207 invitations to purchase: any information giving a product's characteristics and price (a shelf price, an online listing, an email or text promotion, a social media post) is an invitation to purchase, and must clearly and in good time show the main characteristics, the total price including mandatory charges, any optional delivery charges, the trader's identity and business address and email, any cancellation rights, and other legally required information; omitting these is unlawful whatever the effect on the consumer. Drip pricing, revealing mandatory fees only as the consumer proceeds, is prohibited.

CMA207 misleading actions: any factual claim about a product should be backed by evidence, or it may be treated as false; true information presented in a misleading way also counts; the overall presentation can deceive even if every statement is true, for example 'Be quick! We've sold 10 in the last 5 mins' when stock is high, or a small-print footnote limiting a discount; relevant matters include price, a specific price advantage, the need for a repair, and the trader's qualifications, approvals and affiliations. Adds a UK basis for the course's 'only state deadlines that are real' advice.

CMA207 misleading omissions: material information includes a minimum contract period or future purchase commitment and that a product is second-hand or reconditioned; information given unclearly, late or where the consumer is unlikely to see it counts as omitted; a practice must identify its commercial intent: a phone 'survey' about home security that turns into a burglar-alarm pitch breaks the rule. Directly relevant to the approach and cold-call lessons.

CMA207 aggressive practices: harassment, coercion (including use or threat of force) and undue influence, meaning exploiting a position of power so as to significantly limit the consumer's ability to make an informed decision; factors are the nature, timing and location of the practice, threatening or abusive language, exploiting vulnerability, threats of action that cannot legally be taken, and onerous steps to exercise rights. Examples: driving a consumer to the bank for cash, a timeshare trip with no transport home unless they sign. Gives the closing and negotiation lessons a legal line between persuasion and pressure.

CMA207 professional diligence: a general safety net requiring the skill and care expected under honest market practice or good faith; a trader should not take advantage of a consumer's inexperience; common bad practice in a sector is no defence, and following a code may not be enough. Fits the course's ethics and personal-code lesson.

CMA207 offences: banned practices (except paragraphs 12, 13 and 30), omissions from an invitation to purchase, most misleading actions, misleading omissions and aggressive practices are strict liability offences, so intent need not be proved; breach of professional diligence needs knowledge or recklessness; a due diligence defence exists; on indictment the penalty can be a fine, up to two years' imprisonment, or both; company officers who consent or connive can also be prosecuted.
CMA207 chapter 9: those who write or monitor a code of conduct must not promote unfair practices in it. Relevant to trade bodies, not to an individual salesperson.
